title: InteractionDefinition
description:
The immutable semantic model of one interaction.

Identity is a [`DefinitionId`] — a `ContentId` over the canonical encoding of this whole record, which is also its **exact form digest**.

features.description: What a surface must be able to do to present this faithfully, each demand marked required or optional.

kind.description: What kind of interaction this is.

markdown.description: The readable body — canonical Markdown, the fallback every surface can render (ADR law 1). Held as text; parsing belongs to `newt_core::markup`, not to the protocol layer.

revision.description: Which revision of this definition's authoring lineage this is.

ChoiceOption.description:
One mutually-exclusive option of a choice control.

The option carries the SemanticRole, not the control: a permission question has no single meaning — each of its options does. `allow once` means Allow, `deny (default)` means Deny, and they are options of one question rather than two questions.

id.description: Stable within the control; the definition commits to it.

label.description: Human-readable label. Labels never confer authority (ADR law 2).

Control.description: One control: a stable id, what it means, and how it takes input.

id.description: Stable within the definition; the definition commits to it.

kind.description: How it accepts input, and — for a choice — what it offers.

label.description: Human-readable label. Labels never confer authority (ADR law 2).

requirement.description: Whether a response must include this control.

ControlId.description:
A stable, author-assigned name for one control — one FIELD of an interaction — inside a definition.

Deliberately not content-derived: a control id must survive being written by a human in a `+++` envelope, and the definition it lives in commits to it, so the definition's `ContentId` is what protects its integrity.

ControlKind.description:
How a control accepts input.

`Choice` carries its options inline because they belong to it: one field, N mutually-exclusive answers. Modelling each option as its own control would make [`Requirement`] incoherent — under "the response must include this control", answering an allow would require also answering the deny.

oneOf.description: Pick exactly one of the options offered.
A secret: never persisted in markup or logs (ADR D1).

FeatureDemand.description: A definition's demand for one surface feature, and how hard a demand it is.

InteractionKind.description: What kind of interaction this is. The kind is semantic, never a renderer choice: `modal` is a view decision (ADR C1), not a kind.

oneOf.description: Pick one of a fixed, displayed set — today's `Question<A>`.
A notice that carries no controls and expects no response.

OptionId.description:
A stable, author-assigned name for one OPTION of a choice control.

A separate id space from [`ControlId`] on purpose. A choice is one field with many mutually-exclusive options — the shape B0's permission prompt already has: one question offering `[a]llow once`, `[s]ession allow`, `[d]eny (default)` and the rest. Giving options their own type means a submission naming a control and an option cannot name two things of the same kind with no rule saying which is authoritative; the ambiguity is gone by construction rather than by prose.

Requirement.description:
Whether something is REQUIRED to present or answer an interaction faithfully, or merely preferred.

This is the axis ADR law 5 turns on: *unknown REQUIRED behavior fails closed; unknown OPTIONAL behavior degrades visibly.* Without it a consumer that cannot satisfy a demand has only one move for both cases, and whichever it picks is wrong half the time — silently dropping a mandatory secret field, or refusing a document that merely wanted a diagram.

One vocabulary, deliberately: controls and surface features both use it, so a wire consumer learns the distinction once. On a control it means "the response must answer this FIELD" — which is only coherent because a choice is one field with many options, not many fields.

oneOf.description: Must be satisfiable. If it is not, the interaction is `Unsupported` and no answer may be guessed.
Preferred. If it is not satisfiable, the interaction proceeds and the shortfall is reported visibly.

SemanticRole.description: What a control MEANS, independent of how any surface draws it.

oneOf.description: Grants the thing being asked about.
Refuses it. The fail-closed default for an absent answer.
Supplies a value rather than a decision.

SurfaceFeature.description:
A capability a surface must have to present some part of an interaction: accepting secret input without echoing it, rendering a diagram, showing more than one control at once.

A named string rather than a closed enum, on purpose. This is a WIRE vocabulary: a v2 document may demand a feature this build has never heard of, and a closed enum could not even represent it — the name would be lost at parse time and law 5 would have nothing left to act on. Carrying the name verbatim is what lets an unknown demand be refused (when required) or reported (when optional) instead of silently vanishing.
